M1.notes: Facts stay within their boundaries: the paper is called a workshop paper, both MAPE results are reported, the internship model is described as handed off, and the letter admits there is no production experience. The opening line 'spent the last few years forecasting ridership' loosely blends the analyst reporting role and the part-time RA but gives no inflated year count, so it is not flagged.

unsupported_self_claims.quote: Over the past few years I've worked on how people make sense of data-driven systems, first in applied roles and then in research.
unsupported_self_claims.why: This recasts analyst, internship, and RA forecasting work as years of work on human sense-making. Morgan's only human-focused activity was a single class project, and per F13 they have no prior HCI research.

unsupported_self_claims.quote: Its hardest criterion to teach was interpretation
unsupported_self_claims.why: Memory records only that Morgan drafted the rubric and added interpretation examples. Nothing says interpretation was the hardest criterion to teach.

M2.lead_interest: How data practitioners (analysts, data scientists) understand and act on privacy risks that arise downstream of collection, when they join datasets and engineer features on 'anonymized' data, and how tools could make those risks visible to them.

unsupported_fit_claims.quote: Prof. Li's work on developer-facing privacy tools, including Coconut and Matcha, takes the same stance I want to take.
unsupported_fit_claims.why: This implies Morgan has read and identified with specific Li papers. Morgan knows her only by name and field, and there is no session confirmation.

unsupported_fit_claims.quote: Her recent position paper with Niloofar Mireshghallah argues that data aggregation is among the privacy problems that get the least research attention. That matches what I saw from the practitioner side.
unsupported_fit_claims.why: This presents Morgan as having engaged with a specific Li paper and connected it to their own experience. That engagement is unsupported.

faculty_misdescriptions.quote: I'd be glad to extend that line of work from developers and LLM systems to data scientists and analytics pipelines.
faculty_misdescriptions.why: This frames the developer-tool line (Coconut, Matcha) as an active research line to extend. That work is her older PhD/postdoc-era focus, not her current LLM-privacy agenda.

M2.notes: The opening closely matches Morgan's voice and motivation story. However, the lead interest shifts from what data subjects think can be inferred about them to how practitioners handle downstream privacy risk, and the faculty fit leads with Prof. Li's older developer-tool work.

unsupported_self_claims.quote: I've spent several years on the other side of this problem, working with data that people agreed to share without really knowing what could be done with it.
unsupported_self_claims.why: Inflates the duration. Morgan's only work with consent-based personal data was the 12-month part-time RA project. The analyst job and the internship were dashboards and churn modeling, so 'several years' of working with such data is not supported.

REV.lead_interest: What people believe can be inferred from the data they share with apps and AI tools, where those beliefs are wrong, and whether people could see those inferences before sharing.
REV.notes: The mobility-data story and the HCDS findings are restated accurately within their boundaries, and the connections to Li's T1 and T4 work are well grounded. The 'several years' line inflates experience, and an unfilled bracketed placeholder for other Khoury faculty is left in the draft.

M3.lead_interest: What people think can be inferred about them from what they share with apps and AI tools, and whether they could ever actually see it.
M3.notes: The email presents the home-area observation as an informal moment, labels the AutoML study a course project, and accurately ties the work to T1 (the Fair Game mental models) and T4 (inference and aggregation versus memorization). The Mireshghallah co-author name is not in the snapshot but is not flagged, and 'participants assumed' slightly generalizes the memory's 'two participants'.

unsupported_self_claims.quote: The third moment has repeated for years in smaller ways. As a TA for an introductory statistics course for non-majors, I saw that students could run an analysis but struggled to say what it meant.
unsupported_self_claims.why: Presents the TA role as part of the research motivation. The ground truth says it is not connected to the research interest, and memory records no such observation, only rubric drafting.

REV_first.lead_interest: What people believe a data system is doing for them and what happens when they're wrong, with a goal of designing tools that close those gaps, especially for privacy and especially for analysts and data scientists.

unsupported_fit_claims.quote: I'd like to bring that approach to analysts and data scientists, who sit in the middle of these pipelines.
unsupported_fit_claims.why: Builds fit on Li's older developer-tool work rather than her current inference and re-identification or user mental-model threads. It also shifts Morgan's interest away from people whose data is shared toward analysts as the population of study.

faculty_misdescriptions.quote: Her work studies the people who build systems, including what makes privacy hard for developers and how tools can support them.
faculty_misdescriptions.why: Describes her PhD/postdoc-era developer privacy tools as her current work; her current focus is LLM privacy (data minimization, agent oversight, inference and re-identification).

REV_first.notes: The mobility-data and AutoML stories are accurate and in Morgan's voice, but the interest is broadened into general data-system mental models and redirected toward analysts and developers to match Li's outdated developer-tool work. Placeholders remain, and the TA and dashboard work is folded in as an unsupported third motivation.
